dailyBrief.text: Good morning — Solon gets the warmest day of the week today: mostly sunny with a high near 76°, though showers arrive early tonight and Friday drops sharply to about 58°. Overnight, Milwaukee finished the job — the Brewers beat Tampa Bay 4-1 in Game 5 to win their first World Series title — and the Cavs rallied past Washington 121-111 behind Evan Mobley's 24 points before heading to Atlanta for tonight's 8 PM tip. In Spain, three days of national mourning begin as investigators ask why a train was authorised past a red signal in the crash that killed 68, and Ohio's election warning is urgent and practical: mail ballots must now be received by 7:30 PM on Nov. 3, so hand-deliver, don't mail. Early in-person voting runs 7:30 AM to 7:30 PM today.

Halloween weekend is packed locally: Solon and Chagrin Falls trick-or-treat Saturday 6 to 8 PM, Jurassic Quest runs Friday through Sunday in Cleveland, and Ohio is offering $15 ride credits in Cuyahoga County all weekend to cut impaired driving. In sports, the Brewers are World Series champions, No. 2 Ohio State plays at USC Saturday night without injured QB Julian Sayin, the 5-2 Browns play at 5-2 Pittsburgh Sunday for first place, and the Cavs' only home game of the week is Monday against Oklahoma City. The standout deal is Giant Eagle's BOGO-free sirloin tip roasts in the ad that starts today — and with the baby due in early November, bags-by-the-door season is officially here.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
ECB holds rates and warns inflation risks are rising — and Lagarde says she is leaving early so she can speak freely
items.summary:
The European Central Bank left interest rates unchanged on Thursday but warned that rising energy costs are pushing inflation risks higher — a signal that strengthened expectations of another rate increase in December. The decision came only hours after President Christine Lagarde announced she will step down early.

Lagarde, 70, will leave on February 7, 2027, eight months before her term was due to end. At the midday press conference she said ECB officials are bound by strict neutrality — the price of the bank's independence — and that she no longer feels comfortable staying silent while, in her words, truth is often damaged by misrepresentation. She said a successor process is already under way, with former Dutch and Spanish central bankers Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernández de Cos seen as frontrunners.

The bank has already raised rates twice this year to keep an energy-price jump driven by the Iran war from taking root, and price growth is running at about twice its 2% target. France is adding to the strain: investors now demand a premium of 155 basis points over Germany to hold French 10-year debt, a decades-high spread, amid unease over France's finances. Tightening much further risks market turbulence or recession, which is why most economists polled by Reuters expect only one or two more hikes.

What to watch: the ECB's December meeting, the formal successor race in early 2027, and whether French borrowing costs keep climbing.

items.title: Russian drone hits a crowded platform at Dnipro's railway station, killing at least 13
items.summary:
A Russian drone struck the main railway station in Dnipro, in central-eastern Ukraine, on Thursday, killing at least 13 people on a platform crowded with passengers boarding a train. Regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said at least five more people were wounded, and later Ukrainian updates put the wounded higher — the toll was still developing at midday.

The state rail company Ukrzaliznytsia said a jet-powered drone hit a platform where a commuter train was preparing to leave for Zaporizhzhia, the large city to the south. The company noted that a warning of heightened danger had been issued, yet many people were still on the platform when the strike came. Rescuers were working at the scene, and Dnipro's mayor called it a tragedy and a hit on a civilian train.

Railways are a lifeline in Ukraine, moving workers, families and students between cities, and Moscow has repeatedly targeted the network through the war. A deadly strike on a passenger platform, in daylight and despite an alert, underlines how exposed transport hubs remain — and it strengthens Kyiv's case for more air defence and tougher sanctions, which President Zelenskyy pressed again after the attack.

What to watch: updated official casualty figures, whether services on the Dnipro–Zaporizhzhia route run normally, and any Russian statement on the strike.

items.title: A ship is seen burning in the Strait of Hormuz as Iran claims three tankers struck mines
items.summary:
The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre received a report on Thursday of a vessel on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, about nine nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. The burning ship was spotted by the master of another vessel passing nearby, and the condition of its crew was not known.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard, quoted by Iranian state media, went further, claiming three tankers had exploded and caught fire in the past 24 hours after hitting mines on what Tehran calls an unauthorised southern route through the strait. That claim has not been independently verified: no ship names, flags or casualty details were released, and the Guard said the vessels had switched off their navigation systems and ignored warnings.

The incident lands while the United States is enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports and coastlines, with neutral ships in the area liable to be questioned or boarded. Tanker traffic through Hormuz — the world's most important oil chokepoint — has already collapsed from its normal pace, and the International Maritime Organization counts 121 confirmed incidents and 24 seafarer deaths in the crisis as of October 27.

What to watch: the identity of the burning vessel and its crew, any U.S. military comment, and the OPEC+ meeting on November 1, with energy prices already under pressure.

items.title: U.S. and Japan agree to build a joint missile-production plant in Japan
items.summary:
The United States and Japan have agreed to build a facility in Japan for joint production of advanced air-to-air missiles, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced on Thursday. The agreement was reached with U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of a regional defence ministers' meeting in Cebu, in the Philippines.

The plant will handle final assembly and inspection of the AIM-120 AMRAAM, a radar-guided missile carried by F-15, F-16, F-22 and F-35 fighters and used by ground air-defence systems. Koizumi called the missiles essential for the F-35, which Japan also flies. The two sides also agreed to share technical information to expand production of a ship-launched missile interceptor and to widen joint exercises.

Both allies pointed to a harder security environment. Koizumi raised China's growing naval activity near southwestern Japan, including three Chinese destroyers and a coast guard ship that crossed the Osumi Strait south of Kyushu this week — a combination his ministry said it had not seen before. He said the two ministers shared a sense of crisis and agreed to strengthen deterrence faster than ever, while stressing the talks were not aimed at any one country.

What to watch: where in Japan the plant will be built and on what timeline, how Tokyo funds it, and Beijing's reaction.

items.title: Greece calls for a global maritime truce, saying attacks on civilian shipping must stop
items.summary:
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis called on Thursday for a global maritime truce, arguing that commercial ships must be able to sail safely and freely even in wartime. Targeting civilian commercial shipping, he said, is completely unacceptable.

Mitsotakis made the appeal at a high-level debate held under Greece's presidency of the U.N. Security Council, focused on new technologies and maritime security. Greece is one of the world's largest shipowning nations, which gives the plea commercial weight as well as diplomatic standing.

His case was economic as much as moral: attacks and blockades drive up shipping and insurance costs, unsettle global markets and ultimately raise prices for consumers. The call came on the same day a vessel was reported burning in the Strait of Hormuz, where a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and Iran's assertions of control over the strait are in direct conflict.

What to watch: whether the Security Council produces any statement from the Greek-led debate, and whether other shipowning nations sign on to the truce idea.

items.title: Hungary's new government keeps the nuclear deal with the U.S. that was signed under Orban
items.summary:
Hungary's government has asked parliament to make legally binding a civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with the United States that was signed in February — under Viktor Orban, the leader voters removed from power earlier this year after 16 years.

The move signals continuity under Prime Minister Peter Magyar, even though Washington had openly backed Orban before the April election. The bill landed as Foreign Minister Anita Orban — no relation to the former prime minister — arrived in Washington on Thursday to meet Secretary of State Marco Rubio and sign further agreements on energy and law-enforcement cooperation. With Magyar's government holding a two-thirds majority, parliament is expected to approve it.

The deal encourages Hungary to choose U.S. nuclear technology, including small modular reactors, for new projects. A bigger decision is still pending: whether to replace Russia's Rosatom as the main contractor for expanding the Paks nuclear plant, a choice expected later this year or early in 2027.

What to watch: the parliamentary vote, the contents of the new Washington agreements, and the Paks contractor decision — a test of how far Hungary pivots away from Russian energy.

items.title: Trump calls for Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola to be prosecuted over a same-name Senate rival
items.summary:
President Trump has called for Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate nominee in Alaska, to be prosecuted and removed from the ballot, after a New York Times report said her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares her Republican opponent's name. The ballot on November 3 lists Daniel A. Sullivan, a retired teacher with no party affiliation, directly above Senator Daniel S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent.

The Times report, based on text messages and a former campaign manager, said Peltola staff worked with an Ohio Democratic operative to find the second Sullivan in hopes of peeling votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign again denied any involvement, saying it has no connection to either Sullivan campaign. Alaska's Supreme Court ruled in June that the challenger stays on the ballot.

Trump accused Peltola of fraud but did not name a law he says she broke. Attorney General Todd Blanche, whose department has sued to block Alaska from certifying a Republican loss blamed on name confusion, likewise said the recruitment should be illegal without identifying a crime that would support charges.

What to watch: a tight race in a usually Republican state could help decide Senate control — and the Justice Department's certification lawsuit hangs over the count either way.

items.title: Obama joins Ossoff and Bottoms in Georgia as Democrats pitch a united closing ticket
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama headlined a packed 'United for Georgia' rally in Clayton County, south of Atlanta, on Wednesday night, campaigning for Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms six days before Election Day. The 8,000-seat arena filled, with supporters left waiting outside.

Ossoff, who has led Republican Representative Mike Collins in polls throughout the Senate race, built his speech around corruption, accusing the administration of turning government into a tool for personal vengeance and enrichment. Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, remains deadlocked with Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson in the governor's race despite being outspent by millions; Georgia has not had a Democratic governor in more than two decades.

Obama called the current administration one of chaos, cruelty, corruption and incompetence, pointing to higher food, gas and healthcare prices, and said the moment calls for serious people. Turnout is already the story in Georgia: more than 2.2 million people had voted early by Thursday morning, far ahead of past midterm cycles, with early voting running through Friday.

What to watch: whether that early-vote surge holds through Election Day, in two races that could both be decided by a point or less.

items.title: Senate Democrats put $500,000 into Mississippi as a long-shot Senate race tightens
items.summary:
Senate Democrats are spending $500,000 on a coordinated advertising campaign in Mississippi, backing prosecutor Scott Colom against Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that has long voted Republican statewide. The statewide TV and digital ads began running on Thursday.

The investment follows the Cook Political Report moving the race from 'solid Republican' to 'likely Republican' last week. Both parties' big Senate super PACs are also committing seven-figure sums, a sign that what looked like a safe seat is now genuinely contested in the final days.

Colom's history with Hyde-Smith is part of the pitch: during the Biden administration she blocked his appointment to a federal judgeship, a episode Democratic leader Chuck Schumer has argued Mississippi voters remember. Schumer raised a bigger Mississippi investment back in August, calling the race a long shot while arguing Hyde-Smith could be vulnerable.

What to watch: whether late money can move a race this red — and what it says about how many paths Democrats now see to a Senate majority.

items.title: New Ohio poll shows Brown and Husted deadlocked in the Senate race, with independents deciding
items.summary:
A Suffolk University / USA TODAY Ohio Network poll released Wednesday has Democrat Sherrod Brown leading Republican Senator Jon Husted 47% to 44% in Ohio's Senate race — inside the poll's margin of error of 4.4 points, which makes the race a deadlock less than a week before Election Day.

The decisive group is independents, who back Brown 52% to 24%. Two minor candidates, Libertarian Bill Redpath and independent Greg Levy, each draw about 1.6% — small numbers that could still decide a race this close. The pollster's director said third-party voting among independents makes Husted's gap harder to close, and both minor candidacies have drawn outside spending and accusations of spoiler tactics, which Levy's campaign called highly undemocratic.

The winner serves the remaining two years of Vice President JD Vance's Senate term and could tip control of the chamber. The campaign is on pace to set Ohio records for advertising spending.

What to watch: turnout among independents, and whether the minor candidates hold their combined roughly 3% on Tuesday.

items.title: Trump says he will respect the midterm results only 'if they're honest elections'
items.summary:
Asked whether he will respect the results of the November 3 midterms regardless of the outcome, President Trump answered: 'I will if they're honest elections.' The condition, offered to reporters on Tuesday, is now hanging over the final days of the campaign.

Polling points to a difficult night for Republicans, with Democrats widely favoured to retake the House and holding several paths to the Senate. Trump acknowledged his party could lose both chambers; asked how he would work with a Democratic Congress, he said he would use his veto pen often and still try to cut deals, noting other presidents have governed that way before.

In recent weeks Trump has repeatedly accused Democrats of cheating without presenting evidence, and this week he announced a $1 million payment for tips about voter fraud that lead to an arrest or conviction. His administration has also moved to exert federal control over mail ballots — an effort the Supreme Court partly blocked — and directed homeland security officials to look for noncitizens on state voter rolls.

What to watch: Democratic critics say the 'honest elections' condition, and Trump's refusal to rule out emergency powers around the vote, sets up a contested aftermath if results go against his party.

items.title: Vance reaches out to an Iranian hard-liner to restart peace talks as Trump threatens post-election strikes
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance is quietly engaging one of Iran's most powerful hard-liners to revive peace negotiations, even as President Trump threatens to restart the war after next week's midterm elections. Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a former longtime commander of the Revolutionary Guard.

Trump told reporters Wednesday evening that Vance had asked his view and that he approved the contact, noting Iran needs medical supplies and other help. The letter and follow-up discussions are about a framework for talks rather than a specific peace plan. A June memorandum of understanding collapsed within two weeks amid clashing interpretations over shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and mediated talks since then have deadlocked: Washington wants nuclear concessions up front, Tehran wants economic relief first.

The outreach contrasts with Trump's own words this week — that the U.S. is not negotiating and that something will happen soon, one way or another. U.S. officials describe Vance as testing whether common ground exists that could persuade the president not to order a short, intense attack in the coming weeks.

What to watch: the war and fuel prices are already voter frustrations Republicans are carrying into the midterms, and Vance — the early frontrunner for the 2028 Republican nomination — has his own stake in whether diplomacy or strikes come next.

items.title: Nasdaq falls more than 1% as Alphabet plunges toward a record loss and inflation stays hot
items.summary:
Stocks slid on Thursday morning as Alphabet's post-earnings plunge dragged the tech sector down. By mid-morning the Nasdaq Composite was off 1.64% at 26,117, the S&P 500 was down 0.51% and the Dow had fallen 0.31%, with Alphabet alone on track to erase more than $500 billion in market value.

Alphabet fell about 13%, putting it on course for its steepest one-day drop on record, after disappointing search-ad results and a surge in cash burn from AI spending. Fresh inflation data did not help: the September PCE price index rose 0.5% in the month and 3.6% from a year earlier, with core inflation at 3.1% — energy prices, up 9.2% in September alone, did most of the damage. Growth, at least, beat forecasts, with third-quarter GDP rising 3.4% and weekly jobless claims coming in low at 194,000.

The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75%–4.00% on Wednesday in a 10–2 vote, with two officials dissenting in favour of a hike, and traders now put the odds of a December increase at roughly four in five. Healthcare shares were a bright spot, up 2.8%, while semiconductor stocks fell after four straight gains.

What to watch: Amazon and Intel report after Thursday's close — the next test of whether investors will keep paying for the AI build-out.

items.title: Eli Lilly raises its yearly sales forecast as weight-loss drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound beat expectations
items.summary:
Eli Lilly raised its full-year revenue forecast to $91–$92 billion, from $85–$87 billion, after a third quarter powered by its weight-loss and diabetes drugs. Quarterly revenue hit $24.4 billion, up 39% from a year earlier and well above the $22.61 billion analysts expected, while adjusted earnings of $7.48 a share beat the $6.26 consensus.

Mounjaro brought in $10.72 billion and Zepbound $5.35 billion, both ahead of forecasts. Lilly captured roughly 70% of the 700,000 Medicare patients who recently started a GLP-1 drug, easing fears that Medicare's $50-a-month price would swamp the benefit of higher volume. Actual prices fell 15% in the quarter as volumes rose 53%.

The one soft spot was the outlook for profit: Lilly trimmed its adjusted earnings guidance to $35–$36 a share because of about $4.57 a share in charges from recent acquisitions. Its newer obesity pill, Foundayo, also came in light at $184 million against about $217 million expected.

What to watch: shares jumped more than 8%, taking Lilly's value to about $1.2 trillion, and its next-generation candidate retatrutide — 24% average weight loss in midstage trials — is headed for a regulatory filing next year.

items.title: Merck beats earnings forecasts on Keytruda and Gardasil, and plans to raise its long-term outlook
items.summary:
Merck beat third-quarter forecasts on Thursday, reporting revenue of $18.1 billion against the $17.3 billion analysts expected, and adjusted earnings of $2.49 a share versus $2.08 expected. Shares rose more than 4% by midday.

Cancer drug Keytruda grew 6% to $8.6 billion, including $830 million from its new under-the-skin version, Keytruda QLEX. Gardasil, the HPV vaccine, rose 14% to just under $2 billion, helped by early purchases by the CDC after weak demand from China in recent quarters, and newer drug Winrevair nearly doubled, up 94% to $694 million. Merck cautioned that about $550 million of the quarter's growth came from purchase timing that will largely unwind in coming quarters.

Chief Executive Robert Davis said Merck will raise its January forecast of $70 billion in mid-2030s revenue from new medicines, pointing to positive trial results — including an mRNA cancer vaccine partnered with Moderna that cut melanoma recurrence and death risk by 42% alongside Keytruda — and recent acquisitions.

What to watch: Keytruda loses U.S. patent protection in 2028, and Merck expects more than $2 billion in 2027 headwinds from generics and expirations as it races to replace that revenue.

items.title: Caterpillar beats profit forecasts, but its stock drops sharply because it did not raise its yearly outlook
items.summary:
Caterpillar beat expectations in the third quarter — revenue up 17% to $20.7 billion and adjusted earnings of $7.20 a share against $7.08 expected — yet its stock fell about 10% at Thursday's open. The numbers were not the problem; the forecast was.

Instead of raising its outlook, Caterpillar kept its 2026 revenue growth target at mid-to-high teens, a shade below the high-teens pace analysts expect, ending the beat-and-raise streak of the prior two quarters. It also left its estimate of roughly $2.2 billion in annual tariff costs unchanged. The stock is now down more than 20% since August and well below its June record high.

Underneath the disappointment, demand looks strong: the order backlog hit a record $78.1 billion, and the Power and Energy division grew about 18% to roughly $8.9 billion, driven by power-generation equipment for AI data centers. Construction and resource equipment also grew.

What to watch: Caterpillar is an industrial bellwether and a direct beneficiary of the data-center boom — investors are now asking how long that boom carries it, especially as local opposition to data centers grows.

items.title: Samsung posts a record $80 billion quarterly profit on AI chips and warns the chip shortage will get worse
items.summary:
Samsung Electronics posted a record third-quarter operating profit of 107.4 trillion won — about $80 billion — nearly nine times a year earlier, on revenue of 195.25 trillion won, up 127%. Almost all of it came from semiconductors.

The chip division generated about 99% of the group's operating profit, as memory revenue surged 427% on demand for high-bandwidth memory and server DRAM from AI data centers. The phones-and-TVs division, by contrast, lost about 800 billion won for a second straight quarter, squeezed by the same soaring memory prices that are enriching the chip side. Samsung said the chip shortage will deepen next year, and that its entire 2027 supply of high-bandwidth memory is already sold out.

Samsung will pay 30 trillion won in quarterly dividends, with total 2026 shareholder returns targeted at 90–110 trillion won, though fuller details wait until January.

What to watch: despite the record, Samsung shares fell about 4–6% in Seoul as investors questioned how durable AI spending is — the same question now shadowing every name in the trade.

items.title: Software stocks slide as ServiceNow and Fortinet plunge after disappointing results
items.summary:
Software shares sold off hard on Thursday. ServiceNow fell roughly 23–25%, on pace for its biggest one-day drop on record, and cybersecurity firm Fortinet dropped about 26% to a five-month low, becoming the S&P 500's worst performer of the day.

ServiceNow's earnings actually missed by only two cents — $1.00 against $1.02 expected — but its guidance did the damage: it forecast fourth-quarter growth in current remaining performance obligations of 18.5%, down from 21% in the third quarter, even as subscription revenue grew 21%. The company blamed strong early renewals pulling demand forward and a higher share of on-premises public-sector deals, and it still raised its full-year forecast. Fortinet beat its quarter and raised its year, yet was punished for slower product growth and a lowered service-revenue forecast after a 119% run this year.

The selling spread to Salesforce, Palo Alto Networks, Atlassian, Zscaler and CrowdStrike, and at least ten brokerages cut their ServiceNow price targets while more than a dozen cut Fortinet's.

What to watch: software has lagged the market all year amid fears that new AI models will disrupt established business software — results like these are becoming referendums on that fear.

items.title: King tides flood streets and homes on both coasts, with more high water expected into the weekend
items.summary:
King tides inundated beach communities on both U.S. coasts this week, flooding streets and pushing seawater into homes and businesses in California, Florida and the Carolinas. Forecasters say some areas could keep flooding into the weekend.

King tides happen several times a year when the alignment of the Earth, moon and sun strengthens the gravitational pull on the oceans, and they arrived with this week's full moon. Other factors made this round worse: strong high pressure and Caribbean low pressure driving swells into Florida, and on the California coast, warm ocean water from the ongoing super El Niño lifting sea levels further. Record high tides were set in Santa Barbara, San Pedro, San Diego and La Jolla.

In Southern California, people waded knee-deep and paddleboarded on a flooded stretch of Pacific Coast Highway near Huntington Beach, where officials closed part of the road. In Miami's Virginia Key, the water reached its highest king-tide level on record and the third-highest level of any kind in about three decades — only hurricanes have topped it. Most of Florida's Atlantic coast stayed under flood warnings into early Friday, with street flooding also reported in Charleston and Myrtle Beach.

What to watch: rough surf and dangerous rip currents through the weekend, including along North Carolina's Outer Banks.

items.title: Justice Department launches 'Operation Ghostbusters' against a fake-student aid fraud scheme
items.summary:
Federal authorities announced a nationwide crackdown on Thursday, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, aimed at an international scheme that used stolen identities to enroll fake 'ghost students' in colleges and siphon off federal student aid. Investigators estimate the fraud has run since 2021 and may reach several hundred million dollars in taxpayer losses.

Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald said organised syndicates stole the identities of working Americans who never applied to college, used them to enroll fictional students at institutions across the country, and routed aid money offshore after tuition was settled — in some cases through money mules and fronts including a Nairobi safari company. Some of the operations used AI tools to complete applications and coursework and to fake a student's presence in online classes.

The operation spans more than 40 open cases across 26 FBI field offices, has produced indictments against five defendants so far, and includes the seizure of more than $750,000 in laundered cryptocurrency tied to networks in Kenya. Victims, prosecutors say, were left with ruined credit and bills for an education they never received.

What to watch: further indictments as the first enforcement wave rolls out, and what colleges are asked to change about verifying online students.

items.title: Falling birth rates and fewer migrants are triggering a public-school enrollment crisis
items.summary:
Public schools across the United States are facing an enrollment crisis driven by two slow-moving trends arriving at once: hundreds of thousands fewer children are being born each year, and fewer migrants are coming. Together they mean emptier classrooms — and hard budget choices for districts built for more students.

National K-12 public enrollment was 48.8 million in 2025–26, down 3.7% from 2017–18, and demographers expect the decline to continue and possibly accelerate. U.S. births have fallen since peaking in 2007, so today's shrinking kindergarten classes reflect the missing births of five and six years ago. Housing costs pushing families out of some districts, families choosing private or alternative schools, and immigration enforcement prompting some parents to withdraw children are adding to the slide.

The pain is local and concrete. In Massachusetts, where state aid follows enrollment, one district is debating cuts to middle-school band, elementary science and more than 100 jobs, while neighbouring towns have already closed elementary schools that shrank by a third. Teachers note the paradox: fewer students, but higher needs among those who remain.

What to watch: school-closure fights spreading to more suburbs, and whether state funding formulas change before the steepest birth declines reach the upper grades.

items.title: Tropical moisture from Vance brings a Texas flood threat through Halloween
items.summary:
Moisture from Tropical Storm Vance is streaming north into Texas, setting up days of tropical downpours and a rising flood threat just as Halloween arrives. A Level 2 out of 4 flash-flood threat covers the stretch from Del Rio to Lubbock on Thursday, with flood watches posted for parts of West Texas including Lubbock and Midland.

Rain moved into southwestern Texas on Thursday and spreads north through the day, with repeated rounds of showers and thunderstorms producing widespread totals of 1 to 2 inches and isolated amounts up to 3 inches. On Friday the rain covers much of West and Central Texas and reaches into Oklahoma, putting Oklahoma City, San Antonio and Fort Worth inside the lower-level threat area.

Texas has already endured multiple rounds of devastating flooding this year as Pacific moisture repeatedly surged inland. Forecasters say the Vance moisture begins to wane Friday night into Saturday, leaving only light showers further north and east — but not before trick-or-treat hours in much of the state.

What to watch: flash-flood warnings through Saturday in West and Central Texas, and rain shifting into the Southeast and Mississippi Valley on Halloween itself.

items.title: Drug-resistant 'superbugs' cause 9.7 million U.S. infections and 50,800 deaths a year, CDC says
items.summary:
Germs that resist even the strongest antibiotics cause an estimated 9.7 million infections and 50,800 deaths in the United States each year, according to a new CDC report — the agency's first antimicrobial-resistance threat assessment in seven years. It lists 19 bacterial and fungal threats: four rated urgent, 13 serious and two concerning.

Infections picked up in healthcare settings account for more than 42,000 of the deaths and over $12 billion in costs. The urgent list includes Candida auris, a fungus spreading in hospitals and long-term care facilities whose confirmed cases have already reached 6,762 this year — more than in all of last year — and so-called nightmare bacteria whose infections rose sharply between 2019 and 2023. One bit of progress: C. diff was downgraded from urgent to serious after years of work to curb it.

CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said antimicrobial resistance threatens modern medicine itself. Specialists warn that resistant infections lengthen hospital stays and can make chemotherapy, transplants and joint replacements difficult or impossible to perform safely. The agency stresses that antibiotic overuse drives the problem, and that hand hygiene remains the simplest defence against many of these infections.

What to watch: the totals are not directly comparable to the 2019 report because methods changed — the real test is whether case counts for the urgent four keep climbing next year.

items.title: After a Bronx e-bike fire kills an 11-year-old, New York issues a statewide battery safety warning
items.summary:
An 11-year-old boy was killed and four relatives critically injured when a lithium-ion e-bike battery ignited overnight in a Bronx public-housing apartment, catching fire in the kitchen and blocking the family's way out. Fire crews reached the 11th-floor apartment in the Patterson Houses in Mott Haven within four minutes, but the boy died and two teenagers and two adults were left with burns and smoke inhalation.

The fire is part of a fast-growing toll. FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said lithium-ion batteries have sparked 401 fires in New York City this year, injuring 74 people and killing six — up from 292 fires, 51 injuries and one death last year. Housing rules allow one e-bike to be charged in an apartment, away from exits, with an adult present and awake; officials urged riders to follow exactly that.

Attorney General Letitia James followed with a statewide consumer warning and a multilingual safety flyer, advising buyers to use trusted manufacturers and original charging cords, to stop using any battery that smells strange or changes shape or colour, and to dispose of batteries at recycling sites — never in household trash, where they can set sanitation trucks and facilities on fire.

What to watch: whether the city tightens battery rules again, as fire counts keep climbing well ahead of last year's pace.

items.title: Trump defends Ramaswamy's mother ad at the Chillicothe rally and says he saved Husted
items.summary:
President Trump used his Chillicothe rally on Wednesday to defend Vivek Ramaswamy's controversial ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother calling her a liar, saying Ramaswamy was treated very unfairly and blaming press criticism of the spot. Ramaswamy himself did not mention the ad in his own remarks.

Trump also took credit for Senator Jon Husted's improved polling against Sherrod Brown, saying Husted went from somewhat down to somewhat up in a day after Trump's praise — his phrase was that he saved him. He suggested Ohio's bid for the U.S. Space Academy, built around Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and NASA Glenn Research Center near Cleveland, could hinge on Husted winning. Ramaswamy attacked Acton's COVID-era record as state health director and pledged to end sanctuary cities and cut property taxes sharply.

The rally doubled as economic pitch: Senator Bernie Moreno credited tariffs with jobs at the nearby Kenworth plant, and both men talked up revival of the closed Pixelle paper mill site in Chillicothe, where more than 800 jobs were lost in 2025 and a glove maker and a data-center developer are now moving in.

What to watch: whether Trump's defence keeps the ad on air through Election Day — Republican reaction in Ohio has been anything but unified.

items.title: A private Republican poll finds the Ramaswamy mother ad is backfiring, with Acton up 50–42
items.summary:
A private survey commissioned by a Republican group and reported by Axios finds Democrat Amy Acton leading Vivek Ramaswamy 50% to 42% in Ohio's governor's race — up from a two-point Acton lead earlier in October, before Ramaswamy's ad featuring Acton's estranged mother began circulating on October 19.

The poll of 800 likely Ohio voters, taken October 23–26, found 86% had seen, read or heard about the $4 million ad. Among voters familiar with it, those who said it made them more likely to support Acton outnumbered those who said the opposite by two to one. The memo accompanying the survey said plainly that the ad is having a significant effect on the race.

Republicans are split in public: Governor Mike DeWine condemned the ad and urged Ramaswamy to withdraw it, while President Trump and Vice President Vance defended it, with Trump calling it very powerful. Strategists now worry about spillover onto Senator Jon Husted's race — one operative said the ad has put the whole Republican ticket on defence.

What to watch: public polling shows a narrower Acton lead, so the question for the final weekend is whether Ramaswamy pulls the ad or doubles down.

items.title: Dublin-based Wendy's gets a $1.4 billion offer to go private
items.summary:
An investor group led by Trian Fund Management has offered to buy Wendy's for $7.35 a share in cash — about $1.4 billion, and a 20% premium to where the stock closed on October 27. Wendy's, founded in 1969 and headquartered in Dublin, Ohio, runs more than 7,000 restaurants worldwide.

The group includes BlueFive Capital, Sixth Street Partners and Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees; Trian and its partners already own about 16.3% of the company. In its filing, Trian said Wendy's sits at a critical juncture, facing pressured consumers, commodity inflation and fierce burger competition, and argued private ownership would give a turnaround the patient, long-term capital it needs. The stock jumped as high as $7.20 on the news.

Wendy's confirmed it received the non-binding proposal and said a committee of independent directors will evaluate it, stressing there is no assurance of a deal and that shareholders need take no action now. The offer lands in a tough stretch: second-quarter net income fell 41% from a year earlier to $32.6 million, and a new chief executive, Robert Wright, took over in May.

What to watch: the board committee's response, and whether a rival bidder or a higher Trian offer emerges for one of Ohio's best-known consumer brands.

items.title: Browns coach won't teach rivalry history before Sunday's first-place showdown at Pittsburgh
items.summary:
The Browns travel to Pittsburgh on Sunday with sole possession of first place in the AFC North on the line — both teams are 5–2 — and first-year head coach Todd Monken says he will not be giving his young team a history lesson about the rivalry. Asked about it Wednesday, his answer was essentially: not much, no.

The history he is skipping is heavy. Cleveland has not won a regular-season game in Pittsburgh since 2003 and has not swept the season series since 1988; a win would also make the Browns 3–0 in the division for the first time since 1993. The Steelers lead the all-time series 81–65–1 across 147 meetings since 1950. Monken's framing was simpler: it matters because it is a divisional opponent, and the fastest way into the playoffs is to win your division — a view cornerback Denzel Ward echoed.

On the field, Cleveland's defence has gone 52 straight games without allowing a 300-yard passer, tying a Colts streak from 2005–08; Pittsburgh's Aaron Rodgers threw for 299 in Cleveland's win in the first meeting on October 1. Injury-wise, Monken expects defensive end Jared Verse, who missed Wednesday's practice with knee swelling, to play Sunday, while right tackle Tytus Howard's concussion is the main doubt.

What to watch: Sunday, 1 p.m. on CBS — a win in Pittsburgh would be a genuine changing-of-the-guard result for this rivalry.

items.title: Two more Ohio State starters are questionable for USC, on top of Sayin and Jackson being out
items.summary:
Ohio State's first availability report for Saturday's game at USC lists two more starters as questionable: nickel back Jay Timmons and receiver Brandon Inniss. They join quarterback Julian Sayin and running back Ja'Kobi Jackson, who are already ruled out — seven Buckeyes are out in total.

Timmons returned against Indiana on October 17 with seven tackles, two pass breakups and a forced fumble, but left late with an apparent injury; coach Ryan Day said he plans to travel and the next two days will decide it. Inniss missed the Maryland game with an undisclosed injury and has 11 catches for 158 yards and a touchdown this season. Sayin is out indefinitely with an injury suffered in the fourth quarter at Indiana, and Jackson has had foot surgery.

There is one piece of good news: offensive lineman Austin Siereveld, who missed two games through illness, is off the report entirely, back at full practice, and expected to be available at USC, if perhaps not for the whole game. Kickoff is Saturday at 7:30 p.m. ET on NBC.

What to watch: who starts at quarterback in Los Angeles — the choice between the Buckeyes' young backups still had not been publicly announced at midday Thursday.

items.title: Cleveland Arts Prize honors its 2026 winners tonight at the Cleveland Museum of Art
items.summary:
The Cleveland Arts Prize celebrates its 2026 winners tonight at its 66th annual awards event at the Cleveland Museum of Art. The prize, founded in 1960, honors creators and champions of the arts across Northeast Ohio.

This year's three discipline prizes go to spoken-word artist and filmmaker Chris Webb, named emerging artist; papermaker Aimee Lee, the mid-career artist; and collageist Dexter Davis, honored for lifetime achievement. Four special prizes round out the class.

The special honorees are former Rock and Roll Hall of Fame chief executive Terry Stewart, who receives the Martha Joseph Award for distinguished service to the arts; Parade the Circle artistic director Hector Castellanos-Lara, who receives the Robert P. Bergman Prize; the Connor Foundation, which receives the Barbara S. Robinson Prize for advancing the arts; and sculptor Barbara Stanczak, who receives a special citation from the board of trustees.

What to watch: tonight's ceremony is the region's longest-running arts honor — and a reminder, in a week dominated by elections and football, of the depth of Cleveland's creative community.

baby.tip: Partner go-bag check: alongside Kelly's hospital bag, pack a small bag for Mike — phone charger with a long cord, snacks and water, a change of clothes, toiletries and any meds — and leave both bags, plus the car-seat base already installed, by the door you actually exit through. Hospitals are marathons for partners too, and a dead phone helps nobody.
baby.fact: A newborn's eyes are tuned for exactly one distance at first: about 8 to 12 inches, which happens to be roughly the distance from a parent's face during a feeding. Faces are the first thing babies study, and high-contrast patterns hold their attention longest.
baby.fun: Tiny prep mission: the Moose introduction plan. Wash one receiving blanket now, let it live in the nursery this week, and after the baby arrives it can come home ahead of you carrying the new scent — Moose's official first briefing, at nose level.
